description: **Presence is now declared, never inferred.** `FlagOpts` is a discriminated union on `presence`: every flag declares exactly one of `{ presence: "required" }`, `{ presence: "optional" }` or `{ presence: "default", default: <value> }`, and `ArgOpts` moves onto the same union with `required?: boolean` deleted. Declaring none or two is a registration-time error, `default: null` is refused with a redirect to `presence: "optional"`, a list or dict flag no longer defaults silently to `[]` / `{}`, a variadic arg cannot declare a default, and a mutex member declares its own optionality instead of receiving a parse-time exemption. An optional flag or arg delivers `undefined` (bools become a real tri-state), and the inferred handler-args type follows the declaration -- which fixes the mutex-member key that was typed as always-present while the parser handed it `undefined`.

**`ctx.provided(name)`, and presence published everywhere it is asked about.** `ctx.provided` answers whether the invocation caused a flag's value -- true for `cli`, `env`, `config` and `implied`, false for `default` and `infra` -- so no handler reconstructs that boolean out of `ctx.source`. `--dump-schema` emits a `presence` key on every flag and arg entry plus a `default` exactly when presence is `"default"` (empty collections included), and the arg entry's `required` key is gone; help renders exactly one presence marker per line (`[required]`, `[optional]` or `[default: <value>]`), with required positionals and declared empty collections now visible; and MCP tool schemas read requiredness straight off the declaration, so a required bool finally appears in `required`.

**A declared default never runs a flag's `validate` callback, and never counts as supplied.** A validator now sees only values the invocation caused -- CLI, env, config or an implication -- so a default the validator would reject no longer fails the parse when nothing is typed. The same one predicate decides presence for `coRequired`, `requires` and `implies`, and it now excludes the `infra` source (a `relativeToRoot` default resolved through a declared root), which is the declaration deciding just as a plain default is.

**README explains the TypeScript-shaped declaration surface.** The package README now states that the TypeScript implementation is not a port of the Python or Go ones: flag and arg options are a discriminated union on `presence` (a `default` beside `presence: "required"` does not compile, and `presence: "default"` without a `default` does not either), the twin command factories narrow the handler's `ctx` so a `.write()` inside a read-only command is a compile error, and what the three implementations hold identical is behavior rather than spelling.

**Choices are a declaration scope.** `choiceFlag(name, choices, opts)` declares a flag whose type is its set of choices, each declared with `choice({ help, flags?, value? })` and owning the flags that exist only while it is elected. The handler receives one tagged value under the selector's own key -- a discriminated union derived from the literal choice map, so `switch (args.via.choice)` narrows and `assertNever` in the default branch is checked by the compiler, with no annotation written anywhere. Sub-flags are never top-level handler arguments at any depth, `provided(record, name)` answers provided-ness inside a scope, nesting is unlimited, and parsing is order-independent: `--subject hi --via email` parses exactly as `--via email --subject hi` does. A flag supplied outside its elected scope is its own parse error naming the flag, its owning choice and the choice that was elected -- never "unknown flag". A selector declares `required` or a `default` and never `optional`, a defaulted selection must be complete, and `choices` entries become `{ value, help? }` records with the bare-value spelling deleted -- `choices: ["a", "b"]` becomes `choices: [{ value: "a" }, { value: "b" }]`, and a flag whose entries carry help renders as an indented block instead of the one-line `[choices: a, b]` form.

**`mutexGroup` is removed.** Exactly-one-of-these is a member-spelled choice flag now: `memberChoiceFlag(name, choices, opts)` spells each choice as its own flag carrying its own payload, and it reproduces the mutex error sentences and the `--no-x` decline semantics byte-for-byte. There is no shim and no deprecation period -- replace `mutex: [mutexGroup({ a, b })]` with a `memberChoiceFlag` entry in the command's `flags` map. A member gains what a group could not express: a scope of its own, so `--profile work --create-missing` parses and `--all-profiles --create-missing` is a scope error, and a payload carried in the alternative that owns it, so the sentinel defaults on flags that meant nothing unless elected disappear. The handler receives one tagged record instead of one value per member, a member flag is `required once this member is elected` (inverting the rule that forbade requiredness on a member), and the `Flags (mutually exclusive):` help section is gone with the construct. Dependency constraints now operate at root scope only: naming a scoped flag from `requires`, `coRequired` or `implies` is a registration error, because the scope already is the constraint.

**The scope rule reaches the type system and the machine boundary.** A computed choice key is a compile error naming itself (it would silently degrade the delivered tag to `string` and make `assertNever` accept anything), a selector's `default` is typed `keyof C & string` so naming a choice that does not exist fails to compile before it fails to register, and a scoped sub-flag is unreachable as a top-level handler argument -- which is the structural fix for the handler-args unsoundness the mutex-member shape carried. Over MCP one command is still one tool: the selector contributes an `enum` property, every scoped flag contributes a top-level property that never appears in `required` (its requiredness is conditional), and the scope structure rides the tool description as a deterministic `Scoped parameters (enforced at call time):` block. A wrong combination is refused at call time with the same sentence the CLI parser gives.

**A structural parse problem is now reported ahead of a value that will not parse.** An unknown flag, an unknown choice and a scope violation are facts about the command line's shape, and shape is decided before any token's text is interpreted -- on every command, not only on one that declares a choice flag. `myapp cmd --count abc --unknown` reported `--count: expected integer, got 'abc'` and now reports `unknown flag '--unknown'`, and the answer no longer depends on which token came first.

**An integer `choices` entry beyond ±2^53 is refused at registration.** The dumped schema publishes a declaration's choices as a JSON Schema `enum`, and a reader that parses JSON numbers as IEEE-754 doubles -- which every reader of a schema file is entitled to be -- reads a different integer back. Declare a big identifier as a string instead. Float choices are unaffected: the canonical float form round-trips exactly, so nothing is lost there.

**`--dump-schema` writes schema version 2.** A flag or arg entry carries a real JSON Schema fragment under `value_schema`, from a closed subset of `type`, `items`, `additionalProperties` and `enum` with JSON Schema's own type names; the `type` key and the `repeatable` key are gone, because arity is a property of the value and a variadic arg publishes the same array fragment a `list[T]` flag does. A value flag's `choices` splits in two: the values as an `enum` inside the fragment, and the value-plus-help records beside it under `choices` (`help` omitted when an entry declares none). A choice flag has no fragment at all -- its value is a variant the subset cannot express -- and instead publishes its nested choices and scopes, each scoped entry a full flag entry, with `elect_by` as the discriminator. Every entity's keys are emitted in a declared order, the document is written in one canonical encoding so two implementations' dumps are byte-comparable, and the `defaults` block is rewritten as the complete map of what an omitted key means. The dump also stops being blind to behavior: `config_format`, `config_path`, `config_conflict_mode`, per-flag `prefixed` and per-command `flag_sets` each appear exactly when a declaration departs from the framework's own behavior, `config_path` publishes the declaration rather than the machine's resolution of it, and the `checks` block is a function of the declaration alone.

**The MCP tool schema describes array parameters correctly.** A parameter whose value is a list carried its `enum` at the property root, which said the array itself had to equal one of the choices; it now sits inside `items`, describing an element. The projection derives its shape from the same arity rule the dumped `value_schema` fragment states, so a tool schema and a dumped schema cannot disagree.

**A variadic positional arg accepts a list carrier.** `arg("files", t.list(t.str), { variadic: true, ... })` registers beside the element-carrier spelling `arg("files", t.str, { variadic: true, ... })`; both deliver the same array and publish the same schema fragment. The element spelling stays legal and stays the idiomatic one -- this widens the surface, it does not replace it. A list carrier on a non-variadic arg is still refused, and a dict carrier is refused on both.

**A positional arg with helped choices renders an indented block.** The block rule was always content-keyed -- any `choices` entry carrying help -- and it now reaches positional args exactly as it reaches flags: the entries render beneath the arg's line with their help, the one-line `[choices: a, b]` part is dropped in that form, and one alignment column is computed across the whole `Arguments:` section. A defaulted choice flag also renders its complete elected value (`[default: webhook (url=..., retries=5)]`) instead of the bare choice name, and a member-spelled choice flag's line carries its bare name with each member line ending in its own presence part.

**A member's payload property elects that member over MCP and `asTools`.** The flat machine form has no tokens, so supplying the property that flattens under a member's own flag name is that election: `{"profile": "work"}` now elects `--profile` and carries its value, exactly as `--profile work` does on the command line, without repeating the choice under the selector's own property. Supplying one member's payload beside a selector property naming a different member is a double election and is refused with the CLI's own sentence -- `--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive` -- instead of a scope refusal that named the member's own election as the scope it was missing from. One level down the same rule holds: a payload key under an unelected outer scope names that outer scope, byte-for-byte as the parser does.

**A member name colliding with a command-level flag is reported as the duplicate flag name it is.** Electing a member IS the election, so a member's own name is a root token that opens no scope of its own. Declaring `memberChoiceFlag("mode", { profile: ... })` beside a command flag named `profile` -- or two member-spelled choice flags that both declare a `profile` member -- now raises `command "run": duplicate flag name "profile"` instead of the simultaneously-electable message, which could only state the collision with two empty scope paths. A member may still carry its own selector's name, which is never typed under member spelling, and a nested member colliding with a command-level flag keeps the scoped diagnosis.

**A refusal inside nested scopes names the outermost election that came from outside the command line.** A required sub-flag missing under two nested choice flags blamed the innermost election, so a scope elected from an environment variable beside a typed inner one said nothing at all about the variable that caused it. The clause now walks the scope path outermost first and names the first election that did not come from the command line -- `(elected from env var 'MYAPP_VISIBILITY')` -- and stays absent when every election on the path was typed.

**A choice name must match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`, checked at registration.** A choice name is a surface name whatever elects it -- a token-spelled choice flag publishes it in an enum, a member-spelled one puts it on the command line as a flag -- and TypeScript spells it as a property key of the choice map, which constrains nothing. `choice({...})` under a key like `Email`, `e_mail` or `1email` is now refused with `Flag "via": choice name "Email" must match [a-z][a-z0-9-]*` in both spellings, before member spelling's flag-name bans, so a name that fails both is reported as the charset failure it is.

**The README documents the choice flag.** A new section shows `choiceFlag`/`memberChoiceFlag` and `choice`, the derived discriminated union a `switch` narrows with `assertNever`, the compile-checked `default` typed `keyof C & string`, and the fact that `optional` has no union member at all; the feature list gains a choice-flag entry and drops the retired mutex one.

**The flat machine form MCP and `asTools` take answers with the command line's own sentences.** Three refusals were wrong at that boundary. Elections ran one selector at a time, so an earlier selector's missing election was reported ahead of a later one's double election -- `{target: "all-profiles", profile: "work"}` on a command declaring a required `mode` first said `one of --fast, --slow is required` where the same command line says `--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive`; every election now resolves command-wide, at every depth, before any scope, value or presence problem is reported. Electing a payload-carrying member through the selector's own key without its payload -- `{target: "profile"}` -- said `flag '--profile' is required under '--profile'`, naming the flag as its own owner, and is now `flag '--profile' requires a value`. And a payload-less member's own property was ignored, so `{all_profiles: true}` was refused with `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required` where `--all-profiles` elects; it now elects on `true` and declines on `false` exactly as `--no-all-profiles` does, decline clause and redundant-negation refusal included. A selector one level down also names the scope it sits in when it refuses, as it does on the command line.
